name: proximal hamstring tendinopathy
specialty: sports and exercise medicine / orthopaedic surgery

clinicalPearls: Presents as deep, localised lower buttock pain at the ischial tuberosity that is characteristically aggravated by sitting on hard surfaces and by running, lunging and accelerating.
Onset is usually insidious and overuse-related, and it is common in distance runners, sprinters and hurdlers.
Pain is reproduced by resisted knee flexion and hip extension and by loaded lengthening of the hamstrings, and localises precisely to the ischial origin.
Provocation tests such as the Puranen-Orava test, the bent-knee stretch test and the modified bent-knee stretch test help confirm the site.
There is a compressive enthesopathic component, as the tendon is loaded against the ischial tuberosity in deep hip flexion, which explains aggravation by sitting and by hip-flexed activities.
The sciatic nerve lies immediately deep and lateral to the origin, so peritendinous scarring can generate referred posterior thigh symptoms.

Management centres on load management and progressive tendon loading, using isometric then heavy slow or eccentric resistance while correcting lumbopelvic mechanics and initially minimising compressive positions.
Recalcitrant cases may be treated with extracorporeal shockwave therapy or peritendinous injections; surgical debridement or reattachment is rarely required.
reference.pathophysiology: Repetitive tensile and compressive loading of the conjoint proximal hamstring origin on the ischial tuberosity provokes a failed healing response rather than true inflammation. Histologically there is collagen disorganisation, increased ground substance with mucoid degeneration, and neovascularisation with accompanying neural ingrowth. A compressive, insertional element arises because the tendon is loaded against the bony tuberosity when the hip is flexed, so activities and postures combining flexion with load are particularly provocative. Because the sciatic nerve runs immediately deep and lateral to the enthesis, peritendinous thickening and scarring may tether or irritate the nerve and contribute to posterior thigh symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Partial or complete proximal hamstring avulsion
Deep gluteal syndrome with sciatic nerve entrapment
Ischial apophysitis or apophyseal avulsion in adolescents
Referred pain from the sacroiliac joint
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the pelvis and proximal thigh centred on the ischial origin
Ultrasound to assess tendinosis, guide injection and perform dynamic evaluation
Radiographs to identify apophyseal avulsion, enthesophytes or ischial changes
Clinical and imaging assessment of the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joint
redFlags: An acute painful pop with weakness and posterior thigh bruising, suggesting a proximal hamstring avulsion that may need timely surgery
Progressive neurological deficit in the sciatic distribution
Rest or night pain with systemic symptoms, raising concern for a neoplasm around the pelvis or ischium
An adolescent with acute pain suggesting ischial apophyseal avulsion
reference.prognosis: Symptoms are frequently protracted, but the majority improve with a structured, progressive loading programme over several months. Recalcitrant cases may respond to shockwave therapy or injection, and surgical debridement or reattachment is reserved for the small refractory minority.
pitfalls: Missing a retracted complete avulsion that requires timely surgical repair by mistaking it for tendinopathy.
Injecting corticosteroid close to the tendon and sciatic nerve, risking tendon rupture and nerve injury.
Inadequate load progression or premature return to sprinting, leading to recurrence.
Overlooking a lumbar spine or sacroiliac joint contribution to posterior pain.
references: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
management: Structured, progressive tendon-loading rehabilitation, advancing from isometric holds to heavy slow resistance and eccentric hamstring exercises
Relative rest with load modification, avoiding provocative deep hip flexion, prolonged sitting on hard surfaces and sudden acceleration
Correction of training errors and biomechanical factors, with simple analgesia during the loading programme
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy for recalcitrant cases
Image-guided peritendinous injection (corticosteroid or platelet-rich plasma) where loading fails, taking care to avoid the adjacent sciatic nerve
Surgical debridement or tendon reattachment reserved for the small refractory minority
Referral to sports and exercise medicine or orthopaedic surgery for resistant symptoms
